explanations.answer: He justified himself rather than God
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Elihu burned with anger against Job "for justifying himself rather than God" (Job 32:2). Elihu is Barachel's son, a Buzite, and he's been sitting quietly this whole time. Now he's done sitting.

explanations.answer: He spoke before the older men
explanations.explanation: Close, but it runs the other way. Elihu is the one who held back because the others were older (Job 32:4). The text says his anger against Job was about Job "justifying himself rather than God" (Job 32:2). Job talking before the older men isn't the reason.

explanations.answer: He ignored all of Elihu's advice
explanations.explanation: Elihu hasn't given Job any advice yet. He's been waiting his turn, and he only starts speaking later in this passage (Job 32:4, 6). The reason the text gives is that Job was "justifying himself rather than God" (Job 32:2). That's the whole story on his anger.

Yes, baker. Elihu's anger doesn't stop at Job. He also "burned with anger against Job's three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him" (Job 32:3). That's an angry man with a lot of anger to go around.

It's actually true. The text says Elihu "burned with anger against Job's three friends because they had failed to refute Job, and yet had condemned him" (Job 32:3). So his anger lands on the friends too, not just on Job. Nobody in that room is getting off easy.
That's it. "Elihu had waited to speak to Job because the others were older than he" (Job 32:4). He kept his mouth shut out of respect for their years. That's a lot of patience for one man.

The text never says anything about money. It says Elihu waited "because the others were older than he" (Job 32:4). Age was the reason, not a bank account. I'd have guessed richer too if I were hungry for a quick answer.
Strength never comes up in the text. Elihu waited "because the others were older than he" (Job 32:4). It was about years, not muscles. Nobody was arm wrestling in this story.

Right. Elihu says, "I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know" (Job 32:6). He's being honest about why he stayed quiet. I think that took some nerve to say out loud.

It's true, friend. Elihu says, "I am young in years, while you are old; that is why I was timid and afraid to tell you what I know" (Job 32:6). His age is exactly why he held back. He says it plainly to the older men.
That's the one. Elihu says, "there is a spirit in a man, the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding" (Job 32:8). He's saying understanding comes from God, not just from gray hair.
Not quite. Elihu doesn't mention his father's teaching here. He says the spirit in a man is "the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding" (Job 32:8). The source he names is God Himself.

Elihu is young, but he doesn't point to his youth as the source. He says the spirit in a man is "the breath of the Almighty, that gives him understanding" (Job 32:8). He gives the credit to God, and that's the right call.

Yes, baker. Elihu says, "It is not only the old who are wise, or the elderly who understand justice" (Job 32:9). He's pushing back on the idea that wisdom comes only with age. Note he says "not only," so he isn't throwing the old out.
Elihu doesn't bring up power at all. He says, "It is not only the old who are wise" (Job 32:9). The group he names is the old. Powerful people don't get a mention.
Fame never comes up here. Elihu says, "It is not only the old who are wise, or the elderly who understand justice" (Job 32:9). He's talking about age, not who's got the most followers.

You got it. Elihu says, "Job has not directed his words against me, and I will not answer him with your arguments" (Job 32:14). He plans to come at Job with his own words. He's not borrowing anybody's notes.
Flip that around. Elihu says, "I will not answer him with your arguments" (Job 32:14). He's saying he won't use the friends' arguments at all. He's bringing his own.

Elihu isn't waiting on Job. He's done waiting. He says, "I will not answer him with your arguments" (Job 32:14), and a few verses later he says, "I too will answer" (Job 32:17). His plan is about whose arguments he'll use, not about when Job talks.
Not this time. Elihu asks, "Must I wait, now that they are silent?" (Job 32:16). Then he answers himself: "I too will answer; yes, I will declare what I know" (Job 32:17). He's done waiting, friend.

Right. Elihu asks, "Must I wait, now that they are silent, now that they stand and no longer reply?" (Job 32:16). Then he says, "I too will answer; yes, I will declare what I know" (Job 32:17). His waiting is over.

That's the picture. Elihu says, "my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin" (Job 32:19). He's so full of words he feels ready to pop. I think anybody who's held in a long story knows that feeling.
Good guess, but a river isn't what he picks. Elihu says his belly is "like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin" (Job 32:19). The picture is a wineskin, full to bursting.
Elihu's anger is burning, but this picture isn't fire. He says, "my belly is like unvented wine; it is about to burst like a new wineskin" (Job 32:19). It's a wineskin that can't hold any more.
Not quite, baker. Elihu says the opposite: "I will be partial to no one, nor will I flatter any man" (Job 32:21). He's promising not to take sides. That's quite a promise for a man this fired up.
Yes. Elihu says, "I will be partial to no one, nor will I flatter any man" (Job 32:21). He's saying he won't play favorites. He's going to say what he knows, no matter who it lands on.
